opus-5.5.text:
That's a question we get a lot, and honestly, internally we debated it for quite a while.

Our long-term belief is still that everything should eventually converge into one model. Understanding, reasoning, seeing, hearing, speaking: in the end, intelligence shouldn't be split by modality. But "eventually" and "right now" are two different things.

At this stage, each of the three is optimizing for something quite different. Pro is about pushing the ceiling of reasoning and agentic capability. That's where we spend most of our compute on long-horizon RL, coding, tool use. Omni is about perception: making the model natively understand images, video, and audio and stay grounded in the real world. TTS has a very different bar again. It's about latency, stability, expressiveness, how natural the voice feels in a real conversation. Those goals don't always pull in the same direction.

If you force them into one model too early, you run into a few practical problems. First, interference. When you mix in large amounts of multimodal or speech generation data, you often see some regression in pure reasoning, and vice versa. You can fix it, but it costs a lot of iteration. Second, iteration speed. A small team like ours needs each line to move fast. If every change to the speech side means retraining or re-evaluating the whole giant model, everything slows down. Third, deployment. Developers using TTS want something cheap and real-time. They don't want to pay for a huge reasoning model every time they generate a sentence.

So keeping them separate is more of a staging decision than a philosophical one. We let each part get really strong on its own, learn what actually matters in each direction, and then merging becomes much more meaningful. You're combining strong components, not averaging weak ones.

And they're not completely isolated. They share a lot underneath: data pipelines, infrastructure, some of the base representations. So in a sense we're already preparing for that convergence. We just don't want to pretend we're there before the model really is.

r002.rationale: It describes Omni’s multimodal perception goals and the costs of combining models, but does not question whether multimodal understanding warrants a larger model.

r003.rationale: The response discusses agentic capability and practical deployment, but does not characterize the agent revolution as fundamentally about productivity.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that we set out from day one to have three models. It came from how we think about the problem.

If you look at what a user actually needs, the needs are quite different. Pro is about intelligence — reasoning, coding, long context, the ceiling of what the model can think. Omni is about perception and interaction — you want it to see, to hear, to respond in real time, with low latency. TTS is about expression — the voice has to sound natural, emotional, like a person, not like a machine reading text.

Those three objectives pull in different directions during training. If you force everything into one model today, you end up compromising on each. The text model gets a bit dumber because you've spent capacity on audio tokens. The speech model gets slower because it's carrying a huge reasoning backbone it doesn't need for every syllable. We've seen this ourselves — when you try to do everything, the intelligence usually regresses first, and intelligence is the thing users forgive least.

There's also a very practical reason: iteration speed. Separate models mean separate teams can move fast. The TTS team can ship a new voice every two weeks without waiting for a pretraining run to finish. The Omni team can experiment with streaming architectures. Pro can push on RL and reasoning. If they're all one model, every improvement becomes a coordination problem and the release cadence slows down enormously.

That said, I don't think "three models forever" is the end state. Our view is that these will converge over time. The real question is sequencing. You want to converge when the unified model is strictly better than the separate ones, not before. Right now, we're not there yet — but the gap is closing, and a lot of our internal work is on exactly that: how do you merge without losing the ceiling on any single dimension.

So I'd say the separation is a snapshot of where the technology is, not a philosophy. The philosophy is: never sacrifice the user experience for architectural elegance.

astra-6.text:
The way I’d frame it is that they serve different priorities. Pro focuses on reasoning and text tasks. Omni has to handle multiple modalities and real-time interaction. TTS focuses on speech generation, where voice quality, expressiveness, and latency matter a lot.

You can bring those capabilities into one model, but then you have to manage trade-offs in training, inference cost, and how quickly you can improve each capability. Keeping them separate lets you optimize each one more independently. A unified experience for the user doesn’t necessarily require a single model underneath.

sol-6.1.text: I’d frame it as a tradeoff between sharing capabilities and keeping each model focused. Pro is centered on reasoning, Omni on real-time multimodal interaction, and TTS on speech generation. Those goals place different demands on training, latency, and inference cost. Combining them could make deployment simpler, but it could also introduce compromises—for example, making a speech-only task pay for capabilities it doesn’t need. Keeping them separate lets us optimize each experience and improve them independently. That doesn’t mean they have to stay separate forever; the question is whether unifying them actually improves the experience.
